title: Review My Leadership Project
objective: Review your own leadership project using real aims, decisions, delivery, work with others and feedback, then choose a reasoned next step.

blocks.text: This lesson is Unit 2: Arts leadership, Part 2E: Leadership project review. You will judge how your project went and what you learnt about leading. Your own view must connect to things that actually happened.
Keep this separate from Unit 1: Arts practice and pathways. That unit holds your own arts challenge, event review and arts research. Today you are reviewing your role in the leadership project.
A useful review can show success and limits together. You do not need to claim the project was perfect. You need to explain your choices, their effects, and what you would carry forward.

Staff · Silver Unit 2: Arts leadership; Part 2E: Leadership project review. Source: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Silver and universal rules. Silver is the Level 2 Award in the Arts, qualification 500/9914/0. Keep Unit 1: Arts practice and pathways separately evidenced from Unit 2: Arts leadership. The Unit 1A arts challenge must not focus on leadership; a Unit 2 project cannot replace it. Mark P / A / N per part. One Attempted is allowed PER UNIT; any Not Attempted means Below Pass. Results are Pass / Below Pass. The whole Silver portfolio has a maximum of 20 files, organised by unit and part. Nine cumulative part files or two clearly sectioned unit files are possible layouts, not mandatory quotas. Check the actual total file count and separately locatable evidence for every part. Every locator names the actual file plus page, slide or timecode; “in arts log” is not sufficient. External evidence links must be public. The four assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, planning and review, and communication. Only an adviser trained at Silver may assess, and delivery must be through a validated centre. These are conditions staff must confirm, not facts established by this deck. Moderators check the consistency of adviser marking; they do not reassess the work. Advisers must not write pupil plans, reviews or evidence. Prompt, read or scribe only the pupil’s exact words and confirmed selections, then check them back. Core, Extend and Challenge vary support inside Silver; each retains a full pupil-owned review based on actual project evidence. No public showing, filming, personal disclosure or invented numerical quota is imposed. Fourteen 40-minute sessions support the programme, not the whole 95 hours. Actual guided and independent activity must be arranged and recorded toward the 60 guided and 35 independent hours.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Provide actual 2A–2D records and genuine feedback, plus plain paper. Missing activity remains missing. A preparation review cannot be presented as a review of completed project delivery.

blocks.text: Gather the records of what happened
Open the real plan and records: aim and role from 2A, practical choices from 2B, delivery from 2C and teamwork from 2D. Keep actual feedback beside them.
Use your usual writing or communication tool. A photo, saved message, sample or located recording can recall a decision; your face need not appear.
Choose a moment showing your role or a change. Point to its record. Separate memory from what it confirms.
If delivery has not happened, review preparation honestly and prepare questions for the later review.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Both complete authored examples are visible. They model a review method and must never enter a pupil’s evidence as if the events occurred.

blocks.text: Move from a list of events to a judgement
Read this authored example: “We set out the paper. I showed a fold. The group made shapes.” It tells us an order, but it does not judge the leader’s choices or their effects.
Now read: “My first fold was hard to see. I moved the model closer after someone asked. That helped me explain the base, but I needed to check the back of the group too.”
The second example identifies an action, a response and a limit. It opens a useful question: what record would support that judgement? Neither example describes your project.
With a partner or adult, choose one phrase that makes the second review useful. Explain what a reader learns about the leader, rather than just the finished shapes.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model the difference between observed evidence, interpretation and a proposed next step. Preserve the pupil’s own judgement, including a judgement that a choice did not help.

blocks.text: Link a claim to a real example

Use this teaching example record: Aim — help people make a standing paper form. Role — explain the base fold. Note — “I moved the model after a request.” Feedback — “I could see the fold once it moved.” All details belong only to this model.
A review could say: “Moving the model helped this person see the fold. I responded to their request, so my explanation became easier for them to follow.” That claim matches the feedback.
It could not claim that everyone learnt the fold. One person’s comment does not tell us what the whole group understood. The leader would need other evidence for that wider claim.

blocks.title: Build a judgement from project evidence
blocks.alt: Recall the aim, choose a real example, judge its effect, then decide a next step.
blocks.caption: Make the claim no wider than the evidence supports.

blocks.text: The next step can grow from that limit: “Next time I would check each viewing position before the first fold.” This is a future choice, not a claim that it has already been tested.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Read the actual prompt and choices; support the pupil to commit before checking. Use the item feedback as a model reason, not a judgement on personal taste. Keep real trials, meetings, views and project actions separate from these teaching examples.

data.heading: Separate judgement, evidence and next step
data.instruction: Sort these example review cards. All concern the teacher’s paper-form example, not a claim about your project.

items.label: “Moving the model made my explanation clearer for the person who asked.”
items.feedback: This interprets what the event meant. It needs the actual response to support the judgement.

items.label: “The feedback says: I could see the fold once it moved.”
items.feedback: The quoted response is evidence for this person’s experience, not the whole group’s learning.

items.label: “Before another session, I would check the view from each place.”
items.feedback: This is a reasoned future action. It has not already been tested.

items.label: “My project note records that I moved the model after a request.”
items.feedback: A true project note records the action. Its location lets the reader check the account.

data.discussion: Test one judgement in your own review against the real record. Separate your contribution from the group result, keep feedback attributed and choose a reasoned next step.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Do not invent participant quotations or treat silence as approval. Prompt for the pupil’s contribution and accurate acknowledgement of others; avoid forcing a positive conclusion.

blocks.text: Separate your contribution from the group result
A group artwork shows what the group made. Your leadership review also needs your own role. Choose a decision you made, an action you took, or a response you gave to another person.

Use “we” when the team acted together and “I” when naming your contribution. You can value other people’s ideas without taking credit for them. A shared decision may still show how you listened or helped.

blocks.title: Connect your action with another person’s response
blocks.alt: Your action and other people’s responses provide two views of the same project moment.

boxes.head: MY CONTRIBUTION
boxes.line1: the choice or action I took

blocks.caption: Name your own role within the work of the team.

blocks.text: Feedback can disagree with your first view. You might feel an explanation was clear while a participant needed another example. Describe both views, then decide what the evidence helps you conclude.
If feedback was not gathered, name that limit. You may ask an available participant now, but record the reply only after they give it.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Use actual pupil evidence when available. If it is absent, practise with the labelled model and retain a gap note. The adult must not supply a personal review for the pupil.

blocks.text: Test one judgement with a listener
Choose a real moment from your records. Tell a partner or adult what you think it shows about your leadership. Show the linked evidence while they listen or read.
Ask them to point to the part that supports your judgement. If they cannot find it, decide whether the record is missing, the location is unclear, or the claim needs to be narrower.
Use this prompt if useful: “I think __ because __. My own role was __. A limit is __.” You decide the words and the meaning. The listener can ask a question without rewriting your view.
Keep one change that makes the judgement fairer or clearer. A claim may become smaller and more convincing when you remove something the evidence cannot show.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: All tiers retain the same review coverage and pupil ownership. Scribe only exact words or confirmed selections, check them back, and retain honest limits or missing delivery. Do not turn the model into pupil evidence.

blocks.text: Make your own leadership-project review

Review the project aim and your role. Explain useful practical decisions, what happened in delivery, and how you worked with others. Use real feedback where available. Judge what you achieved, what was limited, and what you learnt.
Choose a next step that follows from the review. Explain why it could help. It may be something to keep, change or check, rather than a claim that you need a larger project.

items: Core · Use spoken answers, signs, a recording or short notes to cover the aim, your role, decisions, delivery, teamwork and real feedback. Link your judgement to evidence, name a limit, and choose a reasoned next step. Check any exact adult scribing.

Extend · Make a connected written or spoken review covering the same project evidence. Separate your contribution from the team’s result, explain achievements and limits, and justify your next step with a real example.

Challenge · Complete the same full review, then weigh a difference between your view and actual feedback or another record. Explain how far the evidence supports your conclusion and how it informs your next step.

blocks.text: Save this work under Unit 2, Part 2E. Give the actual file name and page, slide or timecode for the review and each supporting record you use.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: Record the pupil’s own conclusion and next step accurately. This is substantive Part 2E review work; storing files alone does not perform it.

blocks.text: Explain what your review has changed
Show one conclusion to a listener. Ask what they now understand about your role. If their answer changes your meaning, explain it again or adjust the wording yourself.
Name the next step you chose and the evidence behind it. You can decide to keep a useful approach as well as change something that did not work. Both choices need a reason.

Mark whether the review is ready to check next lesson or still has a gap. Keep the actual gap and the help you need visible. A review of preparation remains labelled as such until delivery can be reviewed.

print.intro: Use your actual leadership-project records to make your own review. Explain the aim, your contribution, practical decisions, delivery, work with others and real feedback. Make a judgement that the evidence supports.
focusRows: The project aim, my role and the records I used
My decisions, delivery and work with others, linked to actual evidence
My judgement of achievements and limits, using real feedback where available
My reasoned next step and actual file-plus-page, slide or timecode locators
tiers: Core · Review the aim, role, decisions, delivery, teamwork and real feedback through accessible answers. Link a judgement to evidence, name a limit and choose a reasoned next step. Check any exact scribing.
Extend · Make the same full review in connected words, separating your contribution from the team’s result and explaining a reasoned next step.
Challenge · Make the same full review and weigh differing real views or records. Explain the limits of your conclusion and the reason for your next step.
checks: The review belongs to Silver Unit 2, Part 2E and describes the pupil’s actual leadership project.
The pupil reviews the aim, role, practical decisions, delivery and work with others.
Judgements use actual records and genuine feedback, with limits or missing evidence stated honestly.
Achievements, learning and a reasoned next step are the pupil’s own.
The saved review and supporting records have actual file names plus pages, slides or timecodes.
